Before diving into each meaning, here is a simple thread that connects almost all uses of this word: a bunker is a strong, enclosed, often partially hidden space — built either to protect something or to store something. Keep that in mind and every meaning will feel natural.
Meaning 1: A Military Shelter or Fortification

This is the most widely known meaning of the word.

A bunker is a strongly reinforced structure — usually built underground or partially underground — designed to protect people inside from bombs, bullets, and other weapons. The walls are typically made of very thick concrete and steel, which means even powerful explosions cannot easily break through them.

Bunkers are used in warfare. Soldiers hide in them, plan operations from them, and survive enemy attacks inside them. During World War II, for example, military leaders on both sides operated from underground bunkers. Civilians also took shelter in bunkers during heavy bombing raids.

The key features of a military bunker are:

  • It is fortified — built tough, not just a regular room.
  • It is often underground — to be hidden and to absorb the impact of explosions from above.
  • Its purpose is survival and protection.

In peacetime, governments and powerful individuals sometimes build private bunkers — called nuclear bunkers or survival bunkers — to protect against a possible nuclear attack or catastrophe. These can be remarkably sophisticated, with electricity, food supplies, ventilation systems, and living quarters, designed to sustain people for months.

"The soldiers retreated to the bunker as artillery fire rained down on the field."

"The government built a secret bunker beneath the mountains to protect officials in the event of a nuclear war."
Meaning 2: A Coal or Fuel Storage Compartment

This is an older, more practical meaning that you'll mostly encounter in historical texts, industrial settings, or aboard ships.

A bunker is a large, fixed container or storage space used to hold fuel — especially coal or oil. Think of it as a built-in bin or chamber where a supply of fuel is kept and drawn from over time.

  • On ships, the fuel tanks are traditionally called bunkers. Even today, the process of refuelling a large vessel is called bunkering.
  • In older homes and factories heated by coal, there was often a coal bunker — a sturdy, enclosed storage bin, sometimes built into a wall or kept outside — where coal was stored and gradually used throughout the winter.

"The ship's engineer checked the fuel bunkers before the vessel set out to sea."

"As a child, it was my job to fetch coal from the bunker in the back garden."
Meaning 3: A Sand Hazard on a Golf Course

In the sport of golf, a bunker has a completely different meaning, unrelated to protection or storage.

A bunker is a hollow, pit-like area on a golf course that is filled with sand. It is deliberately placed as an obstacle — a hazard — that golfers try to avoid hitting their ball into. If your ball lands in a bunker, you must play it from the sand, which is significantly more difficult than playing from the grass.

Bunkers are strategically positioned near the fairway (the main playing area) or near the green (the area around the hole), where they can catch stray shots and make the game more challenging.

In American English, you will often hear the same thing called a sand trap, but bunker is the internationally preferred and more formal term used in the rules of golf.

"Her second shot landed in the bunker, and she needed two more strokes just to get the ball back onto the green."

"The course designer placed bunkers on both sides of the fairway to punish inaccurate drives."
Meaning 4: Any Large Storage Bin or Fixed Container (General Use)

More broadly, bunker can refer to any large, sturdy, built-in storage container used to hold bulk materials — such as grain, sand, or other industrial materials. This meaning is an extension of the fuel storage sense and is common in farming, construction, and industrial contexts.

"The grain was poured directly into the storage bunker after the harvest."
How the Meanings Relate to Each Other

Even though these meanings seem very different on the surface, you can trace a logical connection:

  • The storage meaning came first — a bunker was a large, enclosed container.
  • The military meaning evolved from this: soldiers dug themselves into the ground and fortified the space, creating an enclosed protective structure — essentially a different kind of reinforced "container," but for people.
  • The golf meaning uses the shape: a bunker on a golf course is a hollow pit in the ground, visually and structurally reminiscent of the kind of dug-out enclosure the word originally described.

One Final Note on Tone and Register

The word bunker carries a generally serious or functional tone. In everyday conversation, it most commonly comes up in three situations: news and war reporting (military bunkers), golf commentary (sand bunkers), and historical or industrial discussions (coal or fuel bunkers). You are unlikely to hear it used casually or metaphorically in everyday speech, though occasionally people use it informally to describe any dark, enclosed, or hidden space — "his office looked like a bunker" — meaning it felt windowless, cramped, and fortified.
